title: Did anyone watched Barry Lyndon(1975)? Why do some people support barry?

commenti.body:
Well I wouldn’t be surprised people on YouTube like Barry. Considering all the sigma male stuff online, Barry does fit into that a bit. It’s like how people like Travis Bickle from Taxi Driver. I finally watched it and thought Travis was a weirdo creep. 

Barry’s character has a certain gravitas to it that makes him likeable.

“When I see youtube comments” is the problem.  I wouldn’t expect a strong analysis on the comment section and I would say personally I have never supported or truly emphasize with the character Barry Lyndon, I don’t see how you could root for him for the whole film.

Barry Lyndon as your basically your rags to riches Scorsese movie set in the mid 1700s. I think it’s the same people who watches Breaking Bad and root for Walter White, or Wolf of Wall Street and think Jordan Belford is the goal. Because we see their humble beginnings and some people just agree with everything they do, even where they do horrible stuff
Just as i thought. They root barry cuz he “seems like” the underdog chad type. But in reality he didn’t earn any of that fortune,fame by himself.

Barry is easy to empathise with, he has honour and pride. 

He shows himself loyal plenty of times. 

He give lady Lyndon’s son a shot at him. 

I respect a man like that. 

He is a classical gentleman character.

He earned it by being a con artist, and for some people that's valid. If you can dupe someone out of a dollar, you've "earned" it and they're fools and rubes for falling for it and deserve to be taken.

Barry is kind of a cypher, and it's hard to make out his true intentions in many scenes, leaving to several interpretation possibilities. I also think he's kind of a rube (see: the highway robbery scene, him throwing away his shot before setting terms with Bullingdon)… so he's not outright pitiable but I wish he would just make better choices sometimes.

I think his uncharacteristic act of peaceful sacrifice in the end is what resonates with people.

I think he’s interesting because he was able to see life completely enough to transcend his own selfish nature.

Yeah I think the duel exemplifies his humanity and shows his character development, like it would be perfectly in line for the manipulative Barry Lyndon we’ve seen earlier in the film to not think twice about shooting his step son but instead he treats him with love and mercy. And how does he get repaid? By getting fucking shot. I think that’s the moment when I realized I sympathize with Barry bc he’s made the best out of his lot in life (albeit in a manipulative way) and ultimately retains some shred of humanity only for that to be his downfall

Consider the following thought:

"Hereditary wealth and power are naturally unjust, inhumane, and thus worth exploiting for your own benefit however you can, by whatever means."

Most of us probably think this only applying to Barry's motivation. At least at first. But truthfully, recognition of the amorality of the system, and it's fundamental dangers, should be enough motivation for literally any of these characters to thieve, maim and murder. 

Just because someone is born into wealth does not mean they deserve to keep it—although many narratives would like you to think they do. Money and power wielded without intelligence or ambition deserves to fall to whomever does have intelligence and ambition. At first this was Barry manipulating Lady Lyndon—but Barry proved too complacent, too idiotic to maintain his position. Thus his wealth and power evaporated and he was ruined by Lord Bullingdon.
And they totally identify with him in the first scene where he’s too scared to “find” the scarf between his crush’s tits

The duels are interesting they're traditionally seen as something noble, formal and honorable but they're always riddled with shenanigans or claims of foul play like the sword duels are from a refusal to pay wagers. Redman Barry is a rube who's life was perverted from the beginning by his mother, to achieve social ascension and gain wealth from it. He tried to navigate an extremely rigid and hierarchal social order (contempt for it is sewn from the beginning with the "Enlightenment" title card imposed over a duel). This order is riddled by informalities that prevents our protagonist from achieving his set goals which makes everyone else the antagonist.

I think it’s more complicated—different reasons for different characters. Anyone who’s ever felt like they’re carrying the whole burden for an ungrateful spouse and kids can identify with WW. He’s literally in existential crisis. Then he’s whipsawed by miraculous remission and eventual relapse. To quit while he’s ahead would make perfect sense, but would feel to him like going back to the miserable life he had before. 

Jordan Belfort, OTOH, is just a total sleaze. An entertaining sleaze, but not a person anyone who isn’t also a sleaze could identify with. Likewise Scarface. Obviously the people who see them as heroes were never fit for civilized society in the first place.

But Barry Lyndon is a third case. He’s an idiot and a cypher, but emotionally sensitive. And he lives in a completely amoral universe. The loyalty between him and his uncle is the closest thing to a human institution in the whole world portrayed. When the uncle dies, he’s cast adrift, and reaches out to the next mentor he finds, who unfortunately is a scammer. But it’s understandable he would adapt to his new situation—that’s his nature.
So barry sort of redeemed at the end and people sympatize with the redemption.? That’s a possible perspective. thanks.
